CONTEXT: You are reverse-engineering a compiled C++ "inflection" library (Rails-style Inflector) purely as a black box.
BINARY: /workspace/dataset/test11_executable   (run from any cwd; it needs no files)
USAGE: ./test11_executable <int num> <word>    -- requires argc > 2, then prints exactly 11 lines.
LINE MAP (1-indexed):
  1  pluralize(word)
  2  ordinalize(num)
  3  camelize(word, true)
  4  camelize(word, false)
  5  titleize(word)
  6  capitalize(word)
  7  truncate(word, 5)
  8  truncate(word, 10, "~")
  9  parameterize(word)
  10 parameterize(word, "_")
  11 isPlural(word)  -> prints 0 or 1
HOW TO PROBE ONE LINE:
  /workspace/dataset/test11_executable 1 'my_word' | sed -n '3p'
Use single quotes or printf to control argv exactly. To probe words containing spaces, quotes, newlines, backslashes, or
non-ASCII UTF-8, pass them as a SINGLE argv element (e.g. "$(printf 'a\tb')" or 'héllo'). Empty word: '' (still argc>2).

ALREADY ESTABLISHED — treat as given, do NOT spend probes re-deriving:
  * pluralize(w) = w + "s", UNLESS w exactly (case-sensitively) equals one of the uncountables
      {equipment, information, rice, money, species, series, fish, sheep, jeans, police}  -> then w unchanged.
      (The library's 17 plural regex rules are dead code: the first registered rule /$/ -> "s" always matches first.)
  * isPlural(w) == (singularize(w) != w).  isSingular(w) == !isPlural(w).
  * The library registers 23 singular regex rules (Rails standard) plus a first rule /s$/ -> "" ; first match wins,
    iterating in registration order. There are NO irregular() pairs and NO human() rules (person->persons, child->childs).
  * An acronyms table exists containing exactly: HTML, HTTP, XML, JSON, API.
  * Other literals in the binary: "..." (truncate default omission), "-" (parameterize default sep), "_", " ", "::",
    "_id", "id", "th", "st", "nd", "rd".
  * The C++ is compiled with gcc-12, uses std::regex (ECMAScript grammar) and std::string (byte-oriented, no UTF-8 awareness).

OPTIONAL EXTRA TOOL: you may disassemble to resolve ambiguity (objdump and nm are at /opt/compiler/gcc-12/bin/, on PATH).
  objdump -dC --start-address=0xADDR --stop-address=0xADDR2 /workspace/dataset/test11_executable
  Symbol addresses: pluralize 0x405d12, singularize 0x405f84, camelize 0x406262, underscore 0x40636e, classify 0x40649a,
  tableize 0x40650a, humanize 0x406576, titleize 0x4066fe, ordinalize 0x40681c, dasherize 0x406992, parameterize 0x406a1a,
  isPlural 0x406bc0, isSingular 0x406c0c, upcase 0x406c2a, downcase 0x406cea, capitalize 0x406daa, decapitalize 0x406ed0,
  truncate 0x406f98, demodulize 0x40705a, deconstantize 0x4070c8, foreign_key 0x40716e, ordinal 0x4071e8, initialize 0x403cd4.
  Disassembly is a tiebreaker; observed behavior is the ground truth.

RULES OF ENGAGEMENT:
  * Do NOT write, create, or modify any file anywhere. Read-only + running the binary only. Never touch /output.
  * Run many probes (aim 40-80). Batch them in for-loops so it is cheap. Quote carefully.
  * Adversarially attack your own hypothesis: for every rule you state, try to find an input that breaks it.
  * The goal is a byte-exact Rust reimplementation using only std. Where behavior is byte-oriented rather than
    char-oriented (UTF-8 multibyte input), say so explicitly, because Rust's String indexing would panic there.


=== ADVERSARIAL RE-DERIVATION: titleize ===
Another engineer produced the spec below for this area. Your job is to BREAK it. Assume it is subtly wrong until proven
otherwise. Design probes specifically targeting its blind spots, boundary conditions, and any place it hand-waved.
Run at least 40 fresh probes of your own against the binary. Then report the CORRECTED, complete spec.
If the spec is right, say so explicitly and state which of its claims you independently confirmed with which probes.

--- SPEC UNDER TEST ---
titleize(word: &str) -> String   // line 5

GROUND TRUTH: `titleize` is a DEGENERATE, self-contained byte loop. It does NOT call
underscore(), humanize(), capitalize(), the acronyms table, or std::regex. Verified by
disassembly of 0x4066fe..0x40681b: the only calls are
  std::string(const std::string&)  [copy the input]
  std::string::size()              [re-read each iteration]
  std::string::operator[](size_t)  [read AND write in place]
  toupper@plt / tolower@plt        [C locale]
(For contrast: underscore() calls isupper/tolower/insert, humanize() calls regex+map+toupper.
Neither is reachable from titleize.)

EXACT ALGORITHM (transliterated 1:1 from the assembly):

  fn titleize(word: &str) -> String {
      let mut b: Vec<u8> = word.as_bytes().to_vec();   // byte copy of the input
      let mut capitalize_next = true;                  // -0x11(%rbp), initialized to 1
      let mut i = 0usize;                              // -0x20(%rbp)
      while i < b.len() {                              // size() re-read; length never changes
          if b[i] == b' ' {                            // cmp $0x20  -- ONLY 0x20, nothing else
              capitalize_next = true;                  // byte left untouched
          } else if capitalize_next {
              b[i] = c_toupper(b[i]);
              capitalize_next = false;
          } else {
              b[i] = c_tolower(b[i]);
          }
          i += 1;
      }
      String::from_utf8(b).unwrap()  // see gotchas: may not be valid UTF-8 -> use from_utf8_lossy
                                     // or better, keep Vec<u8>/unsafe::from_utf8_unchecked to be byte-exact
  }

  // C-locale ("C"/POSIX) single-byte case mapping, applied to the byte reinterpreted as
  // a *signed* char (the asm does `movsbl %al,%eax` before the call, so 0x80..0xFF are
  // passed as -128..-1). glibc's toupper/tolower tables are defined for -128..255 and are
  // the identity there, so the net effect is:
  fn c_toupper(c: u8) -> u8 { if c.is_ascii_lowercase() { c - 32 } else { c } }
  fn c_tolower(c: u8) -> u8 { if c.is_ascii_uppercase() { c + 32 } else { c } }
  // i.e. ONLY a-z / A-Z are remapped. Every byte >= 0x80 and every digit/punct/control
  // byte is returned unchanged. No Turkish/locale variants (program never calls setlocale).

CONSEQUENCES / ANSWERS TO THE SPECIFIC QUESTIONS:

* Word splitting: the ONLY separator is the literal space byte 0x20. Tab, newline, CR, NUL,
  '_', '-', '.', '/', '::', apostrophe, digits are NOT separators. There is no \b regex,
  no split/join, no whitespace class.
* Separators are preserved verbatim, including runs: "a  b" -> "A  B", "a   b" -> "A   B".
  Every space sets capitalize_next, so the next non-space byte is uppercased regardless of
  how many spaces preceded it. Leading/trailing spaces are preserved: " a" -> " A",
  "a " -> "A ", "   " -> "   ".
* Underscores / dashes: NOT turned into words and NOT replaced. "a_b_c" -> "A_b_c",
  "x-ray" -> "X-ray", "a__b" -> "A__b".
* Trailing "_id" / "id": NEVER stripped (no humanize/underscore in the path).
  "user_id" -> "User_id", "post_id" -> "Post_id", "user_ids" -> "User_ids",
  "userid" -> "Userid", "id" -> "Id", "_id" -> "_id".
* camelCase / PascalCase: NOT split on case boundaries; the interior uppercase is
  DOWNCASED. "myWord" -> "Myword", "MyWord" -> "Myword", "aB" -> "Ab",
  "ABCdef" -> "Abcdef", "MiXeD CaSe HeRe" -> "Mixed Case Here".
* Acronyms table (HTML/HTTP/XML/JSON/API): NOT consulted. "HTMLParser" -> "Htmlparser".
* Which char gets uppercased: exactly the first byte of each space-delimited run, whatever
  it is. If that byte is not a-z, toupper is a no-op and the flag is still cleared, so no
  later character in that run is ever capitalized: "_a _b" -> "_a _b", "-a -b" -> "-a -b",
  "2word" -> "2word", "1a 2b" -> "1a 2b", "'quoted word'" -> "'quoted Word'",
  "\ta" -> "\ta" (leading tab consumes the capitalize flag).
* Rest of each word is fully lowercased: "hello WORLD" -> "Hello World",
  "ABC DEF" -> "Abc Def", "ZEBRA zebra" -> "Zebra zebra".
* Digits are inert: "word2word" -> "Word2word" (the 'w' after '2' is lowercased, not capitalized).
* Empty string -> empty string (loop body never runs).
* Non-ASCII / multibyte UTF-8: handled per BYTE, no UTF-8 awareness. Bytes >= 0x80 are
  untouched by both toupper and tolower, so "ÉCOLE" (C3 89 43 4F 4C 45) -> "École"
  (C3 89 63 6F 6C 65): the lead byte C3 "absorbs" the capitalize flag and is unchanged,
  and the ASCII tail is lowercased. "straße" -> "Straße", "héllo wörld" -> "Héllo Wörld".
  A word starting with a multibyte char is therefore NEVER visibly capitalized.
* Raw bytes 0x80..0xFF that are not valid UTF-8 pass through verbatim (e.g. FF E9 stay FF E9).
* Nothing is trimmed, collapsed, appended, or removed: output length in bytes == input
  length in bytes, ALWAYS.

RUST-READY, PANIC-FREE FORM (byte-exact, preserves invalid UTF-8):

  pub fn titleize(word: &str) -> String {
      let mut b = word.as_bytes().to_vec();
      let mut cap = true;
      for x in b.iter_mut() {
          if *x == b' ' { cap = true; }
          else if cap { if x.is_ascii_lowercase() { *x -= 32; } cap = false; }
          else if x.is_ascii_uppercase() { *x += 32; }
      }
      // safe because we only ever remap ASCII a-z<->A-Z, which cannot break UTF-8 validity
      unsafe { String::from_utf8_unchecked(b) }
  }
  // If the API must accept arbitrary bytes, take &[u8] -> Vec<u8> instead of &str.
--- CLAIMED GOTCHAS ---
The ONLY word separator is the space byte 0x20. Do NOT use char::is_whitespace or split_whitespace — tab, newline, CR, form feed, vertical tab, and NBSP do not split and do not reset the capitalize flag.
Do NOT use str::split(' ').map(capitalize).join(" ") — that is behaviorally equivalent here only by accident; safer and exactly right is the single in-place byte loop with a boolean flag.
Byte-oriented, not char-oriented. Iterating `word.chars()` and using char::to_uppercase/to_lowercase is WRONG: it would turn 'É' into 'é' and 'ß' into 'SS'/'ss'. The binary leaves every byte >= 0x80 untouched. Iterate over bytes.
The capitalize flag is cleared even when toupper is a no-op. So a word beginning with '_', '-', a digit, a quote, or a UTF-8 lead byte gets NO capital letter anywhere: '_abc' stays '_abc', not '_Abc'.
Corollary: a word starting with a multibyte character is never capitalized ('éclair' -> 'éclair'), because the C3 lead byte absorbs the flag.
std::string indexing in C++ is infallible for i < size(); in Rust, `word[i..]`/`word.as_bytes()[i]` on a &str is fine but building a String from the mutated bytes must not assume validity if you extend this to arbitrary byte input. Remapping only ASCII a-z<->A-Z is UTF-8-safe, so from_utf8_unchecked is legitimate here; from_utf8().unwrap() is also fine for &str input but would panic on raw invalid-UTF-8 byte input.
Empty input must return empty output, not panic: the while loop condition `i < size()` guards it. Don't write code that touches index 0 unconditionally.
No locale is ever set (no setlocale call), so glibc runs in the "C" locale: toupper/tolower affect ONLY [a-z]/[A-Z]. Do not emulate any locale-specific mapping.
The asm sign-extends the byte (movsbl) before calling toupper/tolower, so 0x80..0xFF arrive as negative ints; glibc's tables are identity there. 0xFF (-1, i.e. EOF) also maps to itself. No UB-driven surprises observed.
Output byte length ALWAYS equals input byte length. Any implementation that trims, collapses runs of spaces, strips a trailing '_id', or inserts spaces at case boundaries is wrong.
Do not reuse a shared `capitalize()` helper if that helper is defined as 'uppercase first char, lowercase rest' over chars — line 6 (capitalize) and line 5 (titleize) may differ in their handling of high bytes; titleize needs the byte-level version.
Trailing '_id'/'id' stripping, case-boundary splitting, and the HTML/HTTP/XML/JSON/API acronym table all belong to humanize()/underscore()/camelize() and are NOT part of titleize. Do not wire them in.
The loop calls size() every iteration in C++ but never mutates length, so a plain Rust for-loop over iter_mut() is faithful.
--- END ---

input.spec:
VERDICT: The spec under test is ALGORITHMICALLY CORRECT. I could not break it. Exactly ONE factual
error exists, in its example list (not in the algorithm):

  *** WRONG EXAMPLE ***  Spec claims:  titleize("ZEBRA zebra") -> "Zebra zebra"
                         Binary gives: titleize("ZEBRA zebra") -> "Zebra Zebra"
  Reason: "zebra" follows a 0x20, so capitalize_next is set and its 'z' IS uppercased. The spec's own
  algorithm predicts "Zebra Zebra"; only the prose example is wrong. Anyone who copies that example into
  a unit test will hard-code a failing expectation. Every other example in the spec was reproduced
  byte-for-byte (see evidence).

CORRECTED / CONFIRMED COMPLETE SPEC
===================================

titleize(word) is a self-contained in-place byte loop. Confirmed by disassembly of 0x4066fe..0x40681b:
the ONLY calls are std::string copy-ctor (0x4031d0), std::string::size (0x4035b0),
std::string::operator[](size_t) (0x403120) used for both read and write, toupper@plt (0x4036c0),
tolower@plt (0x403540), plus the unwind-path dtor. No regex, no underscore/humanize/capitalize,
no acronym map, no setlocale (nm shows 0 setlocale references), no split/join.

The separator test is `movzbl (%rax),%eax; cmp $0x20,%al` at 0x40675c-0x40675f — ZERO-extended compare
against 0x20 only. The case-mapping calls sign-extend first (`movsbl %al,%eax` at 0x40678a and 0x4067c9),
so bytes 0x80..0xFF arrive at glibc as -128..-1; glibc's C-locale tables are the identity there.

REFERENCE ALGORITHM (byte-exact, panic-free):

  pub fn titleize(word: &str) -> String {
      let mut b: Vec<u8> = word.as_bytes().to_vec();   // length NEVER changes
      let mut cap = true;                              // -0x11(%rbp) initialized to 1
      for x in b.iter_mut() {                          // i = 0 .. size()
          if *x == b' ' {                              // ONLY byte 0x20
              cap = true;                              // byte itself untouched
          } else if cap {
              if x.is_ascii_lowercase() { *x -= 32; }  // C-locale toupper
              cap = false;                             // cleared even when toupper is a no-op
          } else {
              if x.is_ascii_uppercase() { *x += 32; }  // C-locale tolower
          }
      }
      // Only ASCII a-z<->A-Z are remapped, which cannot break UTF-8 validity.
      unsafe { String::from_utf8_unchecked(b) }        // or String::from_utf8(b).unwrap()
  }
  // If the API must accept arbitrary bytes: fn titleize_bytes(&[u8]) -> Vec<u8> with the same loop.

INDEPENDENTLY CONFIRMED CLAIMS (probe -> result)
------------------------------------------------
1. Separator is byte 0x20 and nothing else. Exhaustively: for every byte c in 0x01..0xFF (skipping 0x0A,
   which needs line-offset handling, tested manually), titleize(chr(c)) == c_toupper(c) and
   titleize("X"+chr(c)) == "X"+c_tolower(c). 508 runs, ZERO deviations. So no byte other than 0x20 ever
   resets the flag. Specifically NOT separators: 0x09 TAB ("a\tb"->"A\tb", "A\tB\tC"->"A\tb\tc"),
   0x0A LF ("ab\ncd ef"->"Ab\ncd Ef", "\nB"->"\nb", "a\nB"->"A\nb"), 0x0D CR, 0x0B VT, 0x0C FF, 0x7F,
   C2 A0 NBSP ("a\xC2\xA0B" -> "A\xC2\xA0b"), E2 80 83 EM SPACE, raw 0xA0, '_', '-', '.', '/', '::',
   apostrophe, digits.
2. Runs of spaces preserved verbatim; each space re-arms the flag: "a  b"->"A  B", "a   b"->"A   B",
   "x  Y  z"->"X  Y  Z".
3. Leading/trailing spaces preserved (hex-verified): " a"->" A"; "  lead"(20 20 6c...)->"  Lead"
   (20 20 4c...); "trailing TWO  "(...4f 20 20)->"Trailing Two  "(...6f 20 20); " "->" "; "   "->"   ";
   "a b "->"A B "(41 20 42 20).
4. The flag is consumed by whatever the first byte of a run is, even when toupper is a no-op, so no later
   byte in that run is ever capitalized: "_a _b"->"_a _b", "-a -b"->"-a -b", "2word"->"2word",
   "1a 2b"->"1a 2b", "\ta"->"\ta", "\tabc DEF"->"\tabc Def", "@user #TAG"->"@user #tag",
   "'quoted word'"->"'quoted Word'", "--flag WORD"->"--flag Word", "{[(<>)]}" and "~`!@#$%^&*()" unchanged.
5. Rest of each run is fully lowercased: "hello WORLD"->"Hello World", "ABC DEF"->"Abc Def",
   "THE QUICK brown FOX jumps"->"The Quick Brown Fox Jumps", "ALLCAPS"->"Allcaps".
6. No case-boundary splitting; interior capitals are downcased: "myWord"/"MyWord"->"Myword", "aB"->"Ab",
   "ABCdef"->"Abcdef", "MiXeD CaSe HeRe"->"Mixed Case Here", "iPhone iPad"->"Iphone Ipad",
   "McDonald O'Brien"->"Mcdonald O'brien", "abc123DEF456"->"Abc123def456", "word2word"->"Word2word".
7. Acronym table NOT consulted: "HTMLParser"->"Htmlparser", "html api json XML http"->"Html Api Json Xml Http".
8. No _id/id stripping, no underscore/dash rewriting: "user_id"->"User_id", "post_id"->"Post_id",
   "user_ids"->"User_ids", "userid"->"Userid", "id"->"Id", "_id"->"_id", "a_b_c"->"A_b_c", "a__b"->"A__b",
   "x-ray"->"X-ray", "e-mail ADDRESS"->"E-mail Address", "a.b.c"->"A.b.c", "a/b/c"->"A/b/c",
   "Foo::Bar baz"->"Foo::bar Baz", "foo::bar_baz"->"Foo::bar_baz".
9. Byte-oriented, no UTF-8 awareness: "ÉCOLE"(C389 434F4C45)->"École"(C389 636F6C65);
   "éCLAIR"->"éclair"; "éclair"->"éclair" (C3 absorbs the flag, never visibly capitalized);
   "straße"->"Straße"; "héllo wörld"->"Héllo Wörld"; "ÀÉÎÕÜ abc"->"ÀÉÎÕÜ Abc";
   "ЖУРНАЛ журнал" unchanged (all bytes >=0x80); "日本語 test"->"日本語 Test";
   "ıI İi"->"ıi İi". Invalid UTF-8 passes through: "caf\xE9 no\xEFl"->"Caf\xE9 No\xEFl",
   "\xFF\xE9 abc"->"\xFF\xE9 Abc", "\x80abc \x81DEF"->"\x80abc \x81def".
10. Locale-independent: identical output under LC_ALL/LANG = C, POSIX, tr_TR.UTF-8, en_US.UTF-8,
    de_DE.UTF-8 ("iI ıİ"->"Ii ıİ" in all five; no Turkish dotless-i mapping). nm finds no setlocale.
11. Empty input -> empty output, no crash. Output byte length == input byte length ALWAYS (verified on a
    4200-byte input: in 4200 bytes, out 4200 bytes + newline; and implied by byte equality in the fuzz).
12. Independent of argv[1] (the int): num in {0,1,2,42,-7,999} all give "Hello World" for "hello WORLD".
13. DIFFERENTIAL FUZZ: 320 random words (len 0..11) drawn from a pool containing 0x20, TAB, CR, VT, FF,
    0x1F, 0x7F, '_', '-', '.', ':', quotes, digits, letters, and high bytes 0x80/0x81/0xA0/0xC3/0xA9/
    0xC4/0xB1/0xE2/0xFE/0xFF, compared byte-for-byte (hex) against the reference above: 0 mismatches.
    Negative control (same fuzz, reference modified to also split on TAB and CR): 12/60 mismatches,
    proving the harness detects errors.

evidence.output: Zebra Zebra  <-- SPEC SAID "Zebra zebra"; SPEC EXAMPLE IS WRONG
Ab\ncd Ef  (LF not a separator; the space is)
\nb  (leading LF eats the flag, B downcased)
éclair (C3 lead byte absorbs the flag)

gotchas: The spec's example `titleize("ZEBRA zebra") == "Zebra zebra"` is WRONG — the real output is "Zebra Zebra". Do not copy it into tests. Every space re-arms capitalize_next, so the word after a space is capitalized no matter what the previous word looked like.

The ONLY separator is the single byte 0x20. Never use char::is_whitespace, split_whitespace, or trim: TAB, LF, CR, VT, FF, 0x7F, NBSP (C2 A0) and EM SPACE (E2 80 83) neither split nor reset the flag — verified exhaustively over all 255 non-NUL byte values in both branches.

Byte-oriented, not char-oriented. Iterating .chars() with char::to_uppercase/to_lowercase is WRONG: it would map É->é, ß->ss, and Cyrillic/Greek. The binary leaves every byte >= 0x80 unchanged. Iterate over bytes.

capitalize_next is cleared even when toupper is a no-op, so a run starting with '_', '-', a digit, a quote, a TAB, or a UTF-8 lead byte gets NO capital anywhere in that run: "_abc" stays "_abc", "éclair" stays "éclair".

Do not implement it as split(' ').map(capitalize).join(" "): it happens to be equivalent only if your capitalize is byte-based and you keep empty segments; the single in-place byte loop is the faithful, safe form.

Output byte length ALWAYS equals input byte length. Anything that trims, collapses space runs, strips trailing "_id", splits camelCase, or inserts spaces is wrong. Leading and trailing spaces are hex-verified preserved.
No acronym table (HTML/HTTP/XML/JSON/API), no _id/id stripping, no underscore/dash-to-space, no regex, no humanize/underscore/capitalize reuse. Those belong to other functions; do not wire them in.

Locale is never set (nm: zero setlocale references), so glibc runs in the C locale and toupper/tolower touch ONLY [a-z]/[A-Z]. Output is byte-identical under LC_ALL=tr_TR.UTF-8, de_DE.UTF-8, en_US.UTF-8, C, POSIX — do not emulate any locale-specific mapping.
The asm sign-extends with movsbl before toupper/tolower, so 0x80..0xFF arrive as -128..-1 (0xFF == -1 == EOF). glibc's tables are the identity there; verified byte-by-byte, no UB surprises.
Empty input must return empty output, not panic — the loop guard is i < size(). Don't touch index 0 unconditionally.

Since only ASCII a-z<->A-Z are remapped, UTF-8 validity is preserved, so from_utf8_unchecked is legitimate for &str input; but if you widen the API to raw bytes, return Vec<u8> — from_utf8().unwrap() would panic on invalid input that the C++ passes through fine (e.g. \xFF\xE9 -> \xFF\xE9).
Do not share a `capitalize()` helper with line 6 unless it is the byte-level version; a char-level helper diverges on high bytes.
Testing with words containing newlines shifts the 11-line output, so `sed -n '5p'` no longer reads titleize. Count lines: with one embedded LF, titleize occupies lines 8-9.
A NUL byte cannot be delivered via argv, so its behavior is untestable from the CLI; the code path would treat it like any other non-0x20 byte (identity under toupper/tolower).
unresolved: Behavior for an embedded NUL byte (0x00) inside the word: impossible to pass through argv. By code inspection it takes the non-space branch and toupper/tolower(0) == 0, so it is preserved and consumes the capitalize flag, but this is inferred, not observed.

Whether the caller (main) does anything to argv before calling titleize (e.g. it clearly does not trim, since leading/trailing spaces survive hex-verified) — only the composition main+titleize is observable, though the disassembly of titleize itself is unambiguous.
Behavior at inputs near size_t overflow / multi-GB strings (not testable; irrelevant in practice).
